10.1002_smll.75484: Two‐dimensional (2D) network‐structured materials, encompassing 2D polymers and covalent organic frameworks, have captivated researchers with their highly ordered, porous architectures that promote efficient mass transport and versatile functionalities across diverse applications. However, fabricating crystalline 2D network membranes with precise functionalization and ultrathin profiles remains a persistent challenge, often limited by defect formation or scalability issues. Herein, we introduce a novel interfacial strategy employing photo‐triggered [2 + 2] cycloaddition at the air/water interface to synthesize ultrathin (∼1.5 nm), crystalline 2D network membranes from styrylpyridine‐armed monomers. This approach capitalizes on the reaction's topochemical specificity and irreversibility, enabling stable cyclobutane linkages under mild conditions and enriching structural diversity beyond reversible chemistries. Comprehensive characterization affirmed the membranes’ ordered hexagonal lattice with ABC stacking and uniform porosity. As a proof‐of‐concept application in osmotic energy conversion, these membranes yielded a power density of 18.9 W m −2 under a 500‐fold concentration gradient, highlighting their ion‐selective nanofluidic capabilities. The method's novelty resides in its ability to unlock cyclobutane‐based architectures with ring strain for novel reactivity, while offering a scalable platform for enhancements in pore size and charge density. This versatile synthesis not only addresses key fabrication hurdles but also underscores the membranes’ potential in energy harvesting, ion transport, and related technologies.
10.1016_j.ecoenv.2026.120912: Micro- and nano-plastics (MNPs) are ubiquitous environmental contaminants originating from the degradation of plastics and direct release from consumer products. Global plastic production is projected to nearly double by 2050, intensifying human exposure through inhalation, ingestion, and direct ocular contact. This review synthesizes current evidence on the presence, distribution, and health impacts of MNPs in human ocular tissues, their toxicological effects in animal and cellular models, underlying pathological mechanisms, and contributions from ophthalmic materials. A systematic literature search was performed that focused on studies reporting human ocular detection, animal toxicity models (zebrafish, mouse and rat), cellular experiments, and MNPs released from ophthalmic materials, which were included and qualitatively synthesized. MNPs (predominantly PE, PVC, PS, PP) have been identified in human tears, meibomian glands, pterygium, cornea, aqueous humor, vitreous humor, trabecular meshwork and retina at concentrations up to 63.0 μg/g, with particles < 100 µm most prevalent. In animal models, MNPs induce developmental ocular defects, retinal thinning, corneal epithelial damage, goblet cell loss, and blood-retinal barrier disruption. Cellular studies reveal concentration- and size-dependent reductions in viability, elevated oxidative stress, apoptosis, and inflammatory cytokine release. Ophthalmic products including contact lenses, eye drops, and surgical consumables represent significant direct exposure sources. MNPs represent an emerging threat to both ocular surface and intraocular health through oxidative, inflammatory, and barrier-disrupting mechanisms. Reducing environmental and iatrogenic exposure, alongside development of biodegradable ophthalmic materials, is urgently needed to mitigate vision-related risks in an increasingly plastic-contaminated world.
10.1016_j.enconman.2026.122375: Current biofuels are mainly derived from second and third generation biomasses. When used in chemical looping gasification (CLG), biomasses can be converted to undiluted syngas that is ready for conversion to biofuels, while the energy-intense air separation needed in conventional gasification is avoided. This work performs a “cradle-to-grave” life-cycle assessment (LCA) for biokerosene production and use in jet engines. The syngas for kerosene synthesis is generated through CLG technology with ilmenite as oxygen carrier and tablets of two types of microalgae and pellets of wheat straw and forest wood as feedstocks. These biomasses are representative precursors of two generations of biofuels. The LCA model covers all steps from biomass cultivation/growth to the final biokerosene combustion in jet engines. The four biomasses and ilmenite originate from inside Spain, and after production and mining they are transported to produce syngas in a CLG plant that is assumed near Zaragoza in Spain. Downstream syngas processing includes catalyzed Water-Gas Shift, Fischer-Tropsch (F-T) synthesis, Dry Reforming and uncatalyzed Pressure Swinging Adsorption and Refining. The syntheses of catalysts and adsorbents are also considered. The biokerosene is finally transported to a nearby airport for use in jet engines. The European Commission’s Environmental Footprint method with sixteen indicators is employed to study the process’s potential life-cycle impacts to climate, atmosphere, ecosystem, biodiversity, human health and natural resource depletion. Among the four biomasses, the microalgae produced from raceway pounds have the highest global warming potential (19.4 kg CO 2 eq. emissions), and this is followed by the microalgae from photobioreactors (16.6 kg CO 2 eq. emissions). Microalgae from the photobioreactor use the least land (only 83.7Pt), while wheat straw occupies the most land (1770Pt) for production of 1 kg biokerosene. Hotspot analyses are done through subprocesses’ contributions, and the most influencing flows and parameters are identified. A series of sensitivity and Monte Carlo analyses are made to study the indicators’ sensitivity and robustness. Finally, a scenario analysis is performed to find options that could be used to lower the life-cycle impacts with microalgae.
